newsitem.title: GERMANY: France, Germany back spy satellites, arms deals.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany back spy satellites, arms deals.

text.p: France and Germany averted a possible showdown over an ambitious European spy satellite programme on Friday by agreeing to launch the project in two different stages.

Meeting at their six-monthly summit in Nuremberg, President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl reaffirmed their support for the Helios II and Horus satellites to make Europe independent of U.S. intelligence.
"We agree we want the develop the Helios and Horus satellites according to the schedule," Kohl said after more than five hours of talks with Chirac in this medieval city in southern Germany.

Chirac said the two sides had also taken a "historic step" in agreeing a joint defence and security concept meant to more closely coordinate their policies. He said both parliaments had to be informed before details could be made public.

Kohl said problems with Bonn's budget, which had to be pruned to meet the criteria for the European Union's single currency, meant Germany had to delay its part slightly while France could start up soon. He stressed the delay would be short, saying: "This is very, very important to me."
Officials said France would start building Helius II next year but Germany would put off joining the project until 1998.
Officials said defence ministers Charles Millon and Volker Ruehe also agreed to move ahead in joint projects for two helicopters and a new anti-tank rocket.

France has been especially keen to build the Helios II satellite to make Europe independent of Washington's superior "spy in the sky" capabiities. It has made the project a symbol of Europe's drive for its own defence identity.

But the project, which enjoys the political backing of Kohl and Chirac, threatened to fall foul of Bonn's budget problems. Ruehe, whose thinking is closer to that of Washington and NATO, said openly he did not have the funds to build it.

Officials said Bonn must find extra funds outside Ruehe's budget to provide the seven billion marks ($4.5 billion) for its share of the Helios II and get parliamentary approval before actually joining the French in building it.
Bonn is due to fund 10 percent of the project.
On the other projects, the two sides agreed that Germany would buy a total of 212 Tiger attack helicopters while France would take 215, officials said.
Production contracts would be signed soon and each side would first order 80 apiece, they said.
On the NH90 transport helicopter being developed with Italy and the Netherlands, Germany will order 243 and France 160, they said.
Ruehe and Millon agreed in principle to order 6,000 of the new PARS-3 LR anti-tank rocket for the Tiger helicopter, they added.

The officials reported less progress with other projects like a new transport aircraft, for which France has cut its funding, and the GTK armoured transport vehicle, which Germany is developing with Britain and hopes to win French support for.

A joint statement by Millon and Ruehe stressed that a unit of the Franco-German brigade would be deployed on a ground mission for the first time when it joins the SFOR peace-keeping force in Bosnia next year.
They said they also discussed the issue of reforming and expanding NATO but gave no details.
